before.label: Women’s history
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
before.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.

before.label: Historical demography & history of the family
before.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Louis Henry; Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964); Peter Laslett, The World We Have Lost (1965); Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981); Philippe Ariès (1960); Lawrence Stone (1977). Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

women.people: Eight selections add Kelly, Tilly, Scott, Perrot, Davis, White, Higginbotham and Chakravarti while preserving all fifteen existing people. Shared profiles retain contributor roles elsewhere; French-language and Indian historical work broaden the existing African/German selections without claiming global representation.
women.works_and_arguments: Lerner’s blank is filled with the 1986 book and 1988 methodological intervention; her neighboring identity selection is also filled. Rowbotham gains a specific bibliographic record. New works distinguish primary excerpts from metadata and description. Original representative prose remains intact.
women.internal_distinctions: Nine approaches expose earlier labor history, documentary/rights recovery, socialist feminism, work/family, periodization, Black women, regional synthesis, situated lives and caste. Earlier roots survive alongside later arguments and institutional work.
women.incoming_connections: Early individual contributions and environmental/oral-history routes retain their previous qualifications. Oyewumi’s critique adds a specific challenge to universal categories; Mohanty remains separately represented. No incoming theory supplies a sole origin.
women.outgoing_connections: Kelly’s primary opening/note supports a targeted critique of Burckhardt; Scott/Tilly supply a specific family/work contribution. Biography gains Davis’s named project. Chakravarti’s explicit use of Lerner sharpens the existing women-to-gender connection; technological, scientific, African and Workshop routes survive.
women.evidence_and_interpretation: Lerner’s 1988 priorities are situated primary testimony, not consensus or a complete census of scholarship. Regional editions, reprints, indexed metadata and publisher descriptions remain explicitly scoped. Kelly’s and Oyewumi’s positions are not presented as settled conclusions.

gender.people: Chakravarti, Oyewumi, Bourke and Rosaldo add historically specific caste, category, masculinity and anthropological questions. All sixteen earlier selections remain. The field’s paired title continues to distinguish gender histories, racial formation and legal theory.
gender.works_and_arguments: Crenshaw’s and Anna Clark’s blanks are filled; Bourke’s neighboring military gap is filled too. Primary Crenshaw opening and Scott pp. 1067–1068 clarify arguments. Omi/Winant gains a read course extract with explicit edition/pagination uncertainty rather than a falsely exact 1986 passage claim.
gender.internal_distinctions: Five added approaches distinguish class/family, masculinity, colonial categories, caste and Black feminist historiography. The original gender, race and intersection IDs remain. Amadiume and Oyewumi are not assigned one African position.
gender.incoming_connections: Scott’s direct quotation of Rosaldo creates a named anthropology contribution; her direct Foucault reference improves existing evidence. Marxist/feminist productive inheritance remains alongside criticism, with Anna Clark added as a concrete integration of work, family and rhetoric.
gender.outgoing_connections: Bourke replaces a generic military source, and Oyewumi supplies a scoped critique toward women’s history. The identity critique distinguishes Omi/Winant and Crenshaw. Existing STS, social, national, postcolonial, subaltern and Black-history exchanges keep their distinct source limits.
gender.evidence_and_interpretation: Three source grades are upgraded and Scott’s checked scope expanded. Direct reception, primary opening arguments, institutional book descriptions and catalogue metadata are separated. Omi/Winant’s retyped extract and the contested scope of Yoruba categories remain explicit research questions.

women: Read a bounded Lerner primary book passage and a contemporary critical response. The 1988 methodological paper and Chakravarti’s explicit use establish situated arguments, not the validity of every ancient-historical claim.
